conflicts.description: Whether the L&V Games were held in 2020 and/or 2021, and how many editions had run by 2025. Four documented positions cannot all hold: (1) the L&V Annual Trophy appears to carry a shield for 2020 (Voyageurs) and NO shield for 2021 (f_2000, f_2001); (2) the Order of Owens was not awarded in EITHER 2020 or 2021, per both the operator roster and the award paddle which runs 2019 -> 2022 (f_1987, f_1994); (3) Sean Day is documented announcing the overnight camp stayed closed for BOTH the 2020 and 2021 seasons, pivoting to day camps (sean-day.md, CBC-sourced); (4) YMCA Quebec's own 2025 history calls that year the 78th edition, which from a 1947 start requires exactly ONE skipped season across 79 years. If both 2020 and 2021 were lost, 2025 would be the 77th edition.
conflicts.notes: Three readings, none settled by any available source: (a) the Games ran in some form in 2020 -- conceivably at the day camps -- and only 2021 was lost, which would make the trophy and the '78th edition' claim mutually consistent and the Owens gap a separate decision about that award; (b) both seasons were lost and the YMCA's edition count is off by one; (c) the '2020' shield is misread from an angled photograph. NOT auto-resolvable under the standing oral-history-yields-to-documents directive: this is documented-vs-documented (a physical trophy against a published institutional history against CBC-sourced closure reporting), so it requires human judgement. NEXT STEP is cheap and specific: a straight-on photograph of the trophy's final shield row would test reading (c) immediately.
conflicts.resolution: RESOLVED by operator account (f_2007, f_2008): the 2020 L&V Games were played REMOTELY -- volunteer alumni and campers competing in individual and online challenges within socially-distanced 'bubbles' -- and the 2021 Games were not held. Reading (a) of the three offered was correct. This reconciles ALL FOUR previously-conflicting positions rather than overriding any of them: the trophy's 2020 shield and missing 2021 are both correct; YMCA Quebec's '78th edition' for 2025 is correct (79 seasons less one lost); Sean Day's documented two-season overnight closure is correct (a remote competition needed no waterfront); and the Order of Owens' two-year gap is correct and non-contradictory, since that award recognises canoe-tripping leadership which could not be earned without an in-person camp, while the Games could be abstracted online. NOTE ON POLICY: this is not an instance of the standing 'oral history yields to documented facts' directive -- no document was overridden. The oral history supplied the missing context that made four documented records mutually consistent, which is the resolution path a document-vs-document conflict actually needed.

Three readings are open: (a) Garcia's title change to 'Coordonnateur du camp de vacances' in 2012 marks him STEPPING OUT of the on-site directorship into a different job, with Taylor taking the director role in 2013 while Garcia stayed on in the coordinator post until March 2014 -- this would dissolve the conflict entirely and is the most economical reading; (b) Taylor's 2013 start date (oral history) is a year or two early; (c) the roles were genuinely shared or overlapping during a transition. Reading (a) is testable: it predicts the archived contact pages for 2013-2014 list BOTH Garcia and Taylor in different roles. Checking those specific Wayback snapshots is the cheapest decisive next step. Kristen Whitelaw's April 2015 appearance needs explaining under any reading.

positions.claim: Ross Bannerman was Kanawana's director in 1969.
positions.source: inference in directors-index.md from Bannerman's authorship of a 'Report on Kamp Kanawana' (1969), Concordia P0145/12B01

positions.claim: Geoff Anderson was Kanawana's Director in 1969.

conflicts.resolution: Resolved in favour of Geoff Anderson. This is not an oral-history-versus-document case: it is an INFERENCE from one document's authorship versus a DIRECT SIGNATURE in another. Bannerman was Associate Executive Secretary of the Metropolitan Office from 1967 and 'Assistant du Secretaire General' by February 1970, so his 1969 report reads as headquarters oversight -- which ross-bannerman.md had already concluded independently. directors-index.md is corrected: Bannerman is removed from the Camp Directors table and recorded under the association's administrative oversight instead. Worth noting how this was found: the wiki had hedged the claim carefully ('Role title at Kanawana unconfirmed... suggest senior position') and still carried it in a table of directors. conflicts.notes: Raised and resolved in the same pass; recorded rather than silently fixed because the erroneous attribution had propagated into the Camp Directors table and was cited from other articles.

conflicts.attribute: the lake the first camp was actually held on

positions.claim: The 1894 camp was on islands in Lake Saint-Joseph, Township of Howard.
positions.source: 1951 Kamp Kanawana History; QAHN; McMorris thesis; YMCA Quebec

positions.claim: The 1894 camp was first located at Lac la Croix, and Lake Saint-Joseph was secured only afterwards.
positions.source: src_ia_autobiographical_sketch_1919 -- first-person memoir by a member of the founding syndicate

conflicts.resolution: RESOLVED BY OPERATOR (Matt Aronson), 2026-08-14: 'Read Ball's account again - Lac La Croix was the first one they picked until Lake Saint-Joseph was found, which was a better option.' The 1919 memoir is a SEQUENCE, not a rival claim about where the 1894 season was held: the syndicate chose Lac la Croix, the first party went out in 1894, a better location was found 'just a little further on', and Lac St. Joseph was secured instead. This is the third reading the conflict record itself flagged as the one that would dissolve the conflict. The wiki keeps Lake Saint-Joseph for the 1894 camp and now ALSO records Lac la Croix as the originally selected, abandoned site. NEITHER POSITION IS DISCARDED - they describe different moments. Independent support: the memoir's 'property with fishing privileges' at Lac St. Joseph matches the 1894-95 Annual Report's 'leased land from the Government and the fishing rights of a lake near St. Agathe' - the same transaction described in the same terms by an institutional source written within a year of the events. ATTRIBUTION CAUTION: the memoir is not by Billy Ball; Ball appears in it in the third person as a fellow syndicate member.
conflicts.notes: HUMAN DECISION POINT per CLAUDE.md: two documented sources disagreeing, not oral history versus document, so the standing resolution directive does not apply. Arguments each way. FOR Lac la Croix: the 1919 sketch is first-person testimony from a man who was in the room, written 25 years after the events and 32 years before the 1951 history, which is itself a second-hand institutional retelling. AGAINST: 25 years is long enough to compress a site-selection sequence, the author left Montreal for Winnipeg in June 1894 and so may not have been present at the camp itself, and every other source places 1894 at Lake Saint-Joseph. A THIRD reading, which would dissolve the conflict: 'decided to locate' may describe an intention that was revised before the season, with 'the first group went out' referring to the scouting party rather than the campers. The passage is genuinely ambiguous about what happened in which order. Do not resolve by picking the majority; the memoir may be recording a real detail the institutional narrative smoothed away. Concordia's 1893 'Report - trip to St. Agathe' journal (sub-series 12A) is the document most likely to settle it.

positions.source: The Kanawana Annual Trophy, 1966 shield, transcribed from operator photographs [src_photo_lv_annual_trophy]
Kamp Kanawana Annual Report 1966: 'Lumberman and Voyage[ur], with the Voyageurs being victorious' [src_ia_kanawana_annual_report_1966]

conflicts.resolution: RESOLVED BY OPERATOR (Matt Aronson), 2026-08-14: '1966 is clearly Lumbermen (from the photo).' Settled by returning to the object - the 1966 shield is legible in the trophy photograph - rather than by weighing the two accounts. The wiki follows the TROPHY for 1966; standings are unchanged (Lumbermen 41, Voyageurs 37 on read shields) because the roll already carried the trophy's reading. The 1966 season report's text ('with the Voyageurs being victorious') is PRESERVED, not corrected away, per the no-silent-overwrite rule. STILL UNEXPLAINED: why the report differs. The most interesting unexplored reading is that the two sources record different things - the 1966 report lists sixteen all-camp program days, of which the L&V competition was one.
conflicts.notes: HUMAN DECISION POINT: two documented sources, so the oral-history-yields-to-documents directive does not apply. Likeliest explanation is a TRANSCRIPTION error on this project's side -- the roll was read off photographs of a trophy whose shields are partly obscured by a crossed paddle and axe, and four shields already had to be supplied separately for that reason. One look at the physical trophy would settle it. Second possibility: engraving is done after the fact and can be ordered wrongly, while the season report was written by the man who ran the season. Third: they may record different things, since the 1966 report counts sixteen all-camp program days and the L&V format was unstable enough to be formally reviewed in winter 1976. IMPORTANT CONTEXT: three other seasons in the digitized reports -- 1977, 1978 and 1993 -- match the trophy exactly, and the 1978 report's 'Lumbermen won ... again' independently confirms 1977. The roll is not generally unreliable, which is why this single discordant entry deserves explanation rather than averaging. CONSEQUENCE IF THE REPORT IS RIGHT: standings become Lumbermen 40 / Voyageurs 38 rather than 41/37, and every derived figure -- running balance, longest runs, the levelling arithmetic -- shifts one in the Voyageurs' favour.

positions.claim: The camp comprises 1,200 acres of private land and lakes.
positions.passage: RESIDENTIAL CAMPS - CO-ED. CAMP KANAWANA: Run by the YMCA, Kanawana was billed as Quebec's oldest boys' camp until sister campers invaded four years ago. This summer, 90 boys and 90 girls will share the 1,200 acres of private land and lakes, the canoes, sailboats, handicraft shop and other basic camp facilities just outside St. Sauveur.

positions.source: YMCA Quebec, February 2017, and the wiki's site article
positions.passage: Founded over 120 years ago on 550 acres of wilderness north of Montreal, Camp YMCA Kanawana is Quebec's oldest summer camp. It's a microcosm of Canada, where English, French, rich, poor, recent immigrants and locals sing together around the camp fire.

positions.claim: Both figures are correct reports of what was said at the time; neither was ever surveyed. The camp's own literature claimed ~1,000 acres from 1964 to at least 1970, and the 1974 newspaper figure sits at the tail of that period. The first figure derived from a property report -- 537 acres total, 455 of it land -- appears only in 1989.
positions.source: Kanawana... A Place to Grow, YMCA of Montreal / Kanawana Camping Task Force, 1988
positions.passage: Size: This information was taken from a report submitted to the Y from Royal/Lepage in 1989. There was no record found that showed the Kanawana site has ever been surveyed. / Land 455 acres / Lac Kanawana 60 acres / Lac Wilson 17 acres / Lac Rond 5 acres / TOTAL 537 acres

conflicts.resolution: Resolved on the operator's reading (2026-08-25), which the documents support. The 1974 Gazette's 1,200 acres is not a lone outlier and not a resolvable discrepancy about ownership: it is the tail of a period in which Kanawana's OWN literature claimed roughly 1,000 acres, stated in at least six separate documents between 1964 and 1970 (f_2255). The series begins in the same year the Y bought "120 acres of land south of Lac Wilson which connects Kamp Kanawana to Camp Tamaracouta" and sold a portion of it to the Boy Scouts of Canada (f_2252) -- i.e. exactly the southward, Tamaracouta-adjacent direction the operator identified, and exactly the moment the property stopped having a clear southern edge. The 1988 Task Force report then supplies the reason no reconciliation is possible from documents alone: "There was no record found that showed the Kanawana site has ever been surveyed." The first figure traceable to a property report is Royal LePage's 1989 breakdown of 537 acres total / 455 land (f_2253), which corroborates the modern 550-acre figure closely and is the only figure in the whole series with a stated basis. READING (a) IS WITHDRAWN: no land sale between 1974 and 2017 is needed to explain the gap, and none is documented. READING (b) IS ADOPTED in the operator's form -- the pre-1989 figures describe undeveloped area in the vicinity rather than surveyed owned acreage, which is also why the 1974 wording is "1,200 acres of private land AND LAKES". READING (c) IS WITHDRAWN: 550 is close to the one surveyed-adjacent figure on record, not an undercount. A TRAP IS RECORDED SEPARATELY AT f_2254: the same 1988 report contains the line "Between 1,000-1,500 acres", which reads as corroboration of the 1,200 figure and is not -- it is the Task Force's specification for a hypothetical REPLACEMENT site under its recommendation that the Board consider selling Kanawana. That sale never happened. Anyone re-opening this conflict from a keyword search will hit that line first.
conflicts.notes:
Raised by the p_263 dormant-source RALPH loop. Two documented sources, 43 years apart, differ by a factor of more than two on the size of the property, so this is a human decision point rather than an auto-resolvable case. THREE READINGS ARE OPEN and none is yet supported: (a) the camp genuinely sold or transferred land between 1974 and 2017 -- the Concordia finding aid records a 1977 'Proposed two-site operation-Kanawana and Weredale' and a 1980 working document profiling three camps together, so the period was one of active property review; (b) the 1974 newspaper figure is journalistic error or includes leased/adjacent Crown land and lakes rather than owned acreage -- note its wording is '1,200 acres of private land AND LAKES'; (c) the modern 550-acre figure is marketing copy that undercounts. RESOLUTION ROUTE: the camp's own property records, or the 1980 'Camping and The Montreal YMCA' working document at Concordia, which profiles Kanawana's situation directly.

POST-RESOLUTION NOTE ON HOW THIS CONFLICT WAS RAISED. c_026 should not have been raised in this form. Fact f_2127 -- added at v5.27, well before c_026 was raised on 2026-08-18 -- already recorded the full acreage series including the "approximately 1,000 acres" figures of 1964-1970 and the "never been surveyed" line. The conflict was framed as a bare two-way 1974-vs-2017 disagreement because the KB was not checked for existing coverage of the same entity+attribute before the record was written. The provenance pass in verify_harness.py could not catch this: checks H through L measure whether sources were read, not whether a new conflict duplicates knowledge the KB already holds. Check M was added to close that gap.

conflicts.description: directors-index.md carries TWO INCOMPATIBLE TITLES for Nelson McEwen in 1951, in the same article. The directors table states he 'In 1951 became first Metropolitan General Secretary, Winnipeg YMCA, serving until his death in 1956' (sourced to the Camp Stephens Alumni blog). conflicts.entity: Canadian Camping Association (place of the founding meeting)
conflicts.description: TWO DOCUMENTED ACCOUNTS PUT THE CCA'S FOUNDING MEETING IN DIFFERENT CITIES. connections/institutional-lineage/canadian-camping-movement.md states, on the archival holdings, that 'In 1936, the Canadian Camping Association was founded at the Central Y.M.C.A. in Toronto on May 20, with Statten as first president.' Against that, Charles F. Plewman -- a founder, present at the meeting, and the man who produced the association's first bulletin -- told Jay Haddad in a recorded interview on 15 August 1976: 'We did know there were camps in Quebec, so we invited them to a meeting and WE ALL MET IN OTTAWA and decided to have a Canadian Camping Association - and Taylor Statten was its first President.' The interview was printed in Canadian Camping Vol. 33 No. 6 (Winter 1982), pp. 4-5, after Plewman's death on 28 December 1981. Both are documented; the operator directive on oral history yielding to documents does not settle it, because Plewman's account is a documented publication of a recorded interview with a named participant, not undocumented oral tradition -- and because the two sources disagree about what a document says happened, which CLAUDE.md reserves for human review. NOT the same question as the competing 1936/1946/1949 founding DATES, which are tracked separately; Plewman's testimony agrees with 1936 and disagrees only about the city. Possible reconciliations to test before resolving: an organising meeting at Ottawa followed by a constituting meeting at the Toronto Central Y; Plewman recalling the wrong city at 86, forty years on; or the Toronto claim resting on a secondary source that assumed the association's Toronto address. The CCA fonds at Trent University hold the minutes.
conflicts.notes: Found by the full word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 140. HUMAN DECISION POINT under CLAUDE.md: two documented sources disagreeing with each other. Do not silently prefer either in any article; canadian-camping-movement.md now states both and points here. SECOND WITNESS AND A LEADING HYPOTHESIS (added 2026-09-04, issue 142): May Brown -- then director of the YWCA's Camp Oolahwan in Montreal, later CCA President 1965-67 -- said in a 1976 interview printed in Canadian Camping Vol. 34 No. 2 (Summer 1982), p. 4: 'I attended one of the first meetings on the CCA in Ottawa in the spring of 1947; I was really there as a Director of Camp Oolahwan which is the YWCA camp in Montreal.' She says 'one of the first meetings', not the founding, so this does not settle the conflict. But it makes a pattern of four separate items now pointing at Ottawa and at the later 1940s: (1) Plewman's 'we all met in Ottawa and decided to have a Canadian Camping Association'; (2) the Camp Stephens Alumni claim that Nelson McEwen 'founded the Canadian Camping Association in 1946' with Statten, which the article currently explains away as a possible 1946 reorganization; (3) the Newfoundland association's statement that the CCA 'was incorporated by Letters Patent at Ottawa November 5, 1949'; and (4) May Brown at Ottawa in spring 1947. LEADING RECONCILIATION TO TEST: that a body founded in 1936 out of the Ontario association's circle was constituted as a genuinely national, incorporated association at Ottawa across 1946-49, and that the memories, the Letters Patent and the competing founding dates describe one two-stage process rather than contradicting each other. This would reconcile nearly every rival origin claim the project holds. It is a hypothesis; the minutes at Trent (CCA/ACC fonds, Thomas J. Bata Library) are the document that decides it, and a Finding Aid for those archives exists and was circulated to every provincial association in 1981-82. THE ASSOCIATION'S OWN DATING (added 2026-09-04, issue 148): Bruno Morawetz's Archives Update in Canadian Camping Vol. 35 No. 3 (Autumn 1983), p. 13, reports that 'Cliff Labbett, Immediate Past President, is currently canvassing all the CCA Past Presidents for ideas to celebrate CCA's 50th Anniversary in 1986.' A fiftieth in 1986 dates the founding to 1936. This does NOT resolve c_029, which is about the CITY of the founding meeting and not its year -- Plewman and the archival holdings both say 1936. It is recorded here because it is the strongest evidence yet on the separately tracked 1936/1946/1949 DATE question: the association's immediate past president and its archives chairman, planning jointly in the year a professional archivist took charge of the fonds, acted on 1936. It supports the first stage of the two-stage hypothesis above and leaves the second (incorporation at Ottawa, 1946-49) untouched. THIRD CONFIRMATION IN CLEAN TYPE (added 2026-09-05, issue 152): the CCA's own Publications 1984-85 catalogue states the year outright in both languages -- 'The Canadian Camping Association was founded in 1936 as a non-profit organization' / 'L'Association des camps du Canada, creee en 1936'. Unlike the 50th-anniversary planning, this is an assertion of the founding year rather than an inference from an anniversary. It does NOT bear on this conflict, which is about the CITY of the founding meeting; Plewman and the archival holdings both say 1936. Recorded so that the separately tracked 1936/1946/1949 DATE question is not reopened on weaker evidence. A CCA PRESIDENT DATES IT TO c.1947 (added 2026-09-05, issue 156): Douglas G. McEwen, President, writing in Canadian Camping Autumn 1967 and reprinted Autumn 1985: 'For the first 20 years of its life the Canadian Camping Association's strength has lain in strong provincial associations.' Twenty years before 1967 is 1947. This is the sitting president describing the span of his own association's life, from a Manitoba-based executive, and it lands on the later side of the 1936/1946/1949 DATE question alongside Plewman's Ottawa recollection, the Camp Stephens claim that Nelson McEwen founded the CCA in 1946, May Brown's spring 1947 Ottawa meeting, and the Letters Patent of 5 November 1949. REMARKABLY, the SAME ISSUE carries the 1936 dating twice -- Adamson's 'In 1986 CCA/ACC will be celebrating fifty years' and the 1985-86 catalogue's 'founded in 1936' in both languages. The association printed both datings in one issue. That is the strongest support yet for the two-stage hypothesis, since it shows members operating on both datings at once. NOTE, not established and carrying no weight here: Douglas G. McEwen may be related to Nelson McEwen, Kanawana's director c.1927-1947, whom the Camp Stephens Alumni blog credits with founding the CCA in 1946. If that relationship holds, the two McEwens both dating the founding to the later 1940s stops being a coincidence and becomes a line of enquiry. THE FOUNDER'S DAUGHTER SAYS 1938 (added 2026-09-05, issue 158): in the CCA's own 50th anniversary issue, Adele Ebbs -- Taylor Statten's daughter, secretary to the founding circle and the person who kept its minutes from about 1935 -- was asked whether 1933 for the OCA and 1936 for the CCA sounded right. She said "'36 sounds early to me... '33 sounds right", and, on being reminded that her father helped F. M. Van Wagner form the QUEBEC association in 1937, said "well that is why I thought the Canadian Camping Association was not until... my impression was that it was 1938." The interviewer answered "We may be celebrating 50 years under false pretenses, so let's not upset that apple cart," and she conceded. THREE DATINGS NOW EXIST, ALL FROM INSIDE THE ASSOCIATION: 1936 (its 1980s literature and anniversaries), c.1947 (its president Douglas McEwen, writing in 1967), and 1938 (Adele Ebbs, 1986). Her reasoning -- a 1937 Quebec association, therefore a later national one -- is the kind a founding-circle secretary would have, and is again consistent with the two-stage hypothesis. ACTIONABLE: Ebbs says she began taking minutes of the pre-founding meetings of the six private directors (Edgar, Hamilton, Halliday, Chapman, Cochrane, Statten) 'sometime before I got married, and that was 1935'. THOSE MINUTES WOULD SETTLE IT. Ask Trent for them by that description. NOT NEW EVIDENCE, RECORDED SO IT IS NOT MISCOUNTED LATER (added 2026-09-05, issue 159): the Fall 1986 issue shows the 1936 dating being celebrated twice more -- a '50th Birthday Party for the Canadian Camping Association' held at the Moncton regional conference on the Saturday evening of 4 October 1986, cake provided by the New Brunswick Camping Association, and the '50th Anniversary Patrons' Fund' appeal over the names of Janet Adamson and Jack Pearse. Both are the SAME anniversary Adele Ebbs was told not to upset, not independent witnesses to 1936. Counted here as one continuing institutional assertion, not as two more sources. QUEBEC ITSELF DATED TO 1938, AND THE FOUNDING SIX RE-ATTACHED (added 2026-09-05, issue 160). (a) Ken Willis, writing as CCA/ACC Vice-President (Quebec Region) in Winter 1987: 'The organized camping movement in Quebec was born in 1938. Tony Shorgun... is already at work laying plans for the 50th Anniversary of this birth which, obviously, will be held next year.' That is a FOURTH date for Kanawana's own provincial association (against 1937 from the archival holdings and Alta Kahn's 1958 coming-of-age party; the French section's 1958; and the January 1961 amalgamation the ACQ commemorated as its 25th in 1986), and it was the premise of a planned event, not a passing remark. NOTE THE CROSSING: Adele Ebbs dated the CCA to 1938 BECAUSE she placed the Quebec association in 1937; Willis dates QUEBEC to 1938. The two cannot both stand as offered. What they jointly establish is that the 1937/1938 boundary was unclear to the participants -- a finding about the record, not grounds to prefer either. (b) THE SIX ARE THE OCA'S, NOT THE CCA'S. John Gilchrist, independently of Ebbs, named the same six -- Statten, Halliday, Cochrane, Hamilton, Chapman, Edgar -- and the interviewer identified what they formed: 'That was the Ontario Camping Association. Taylor Statten was the first President, in 1933.' So the supper club of private directors whose minutes Ebbs began keeping about 1935 is the ONTARIO founding circle. Whatever happened nationally in 1936, 1938 or 1947 is a separate act, and the six should no longer be cited as evidence about the national founding date. This narrows the question rather than answering it. (c) ACTIONABLE: if the Quebec 50th anniversary was held in 1988 it produced a programme or commemorative publication compiled by Tony Shorgun -- a name new to this project. Tracked in p_319. SHARPENED, NOT ADDED TO (2026-09-05, issue 164): the May Brown item above -- 'May Brown at one of its first meetings at Ottawa in the spring of 1947' -- now has provenance. Interviewed in Winter 1988 she says: 'I was going to be directing Camp Oolawhan for the summer but I was looking for something for the fall so I WAS SENT BY THE MONTREAL YWCA to a meeting in Ottawa which was the first meeting of the... when they were going to establish a Canadian Camping Association. Blackie Blackstock was there and he introduced me to Marion Henderson Penney from U.B.C.' So the person at Ottawa in 1947 was the DIRECTOR OF CAMP OOLAHWAN, sent by the YWCA of Montreal -- i.e. a Quebec delegate. This does NOT add a fifth item to the Ottawa cluster; it makes the existing one more specific and more credible, and it means a Quebec institution has a record of sending someone. ASK the YWCA of Montreal successor and Concordia for 1947 YWCA committee minutes naming that delegation.

conflicts.entity: Alta R. Kahn (years as Executive Secretary, Jewish Community Camps of Montreal)
conflicts.description: TWO PRINTINGS OF THE SAME TRIBUTE GIVE DIFFERENT END DATES. The tribute read on Alta R. Kahn's appointment as the Quebec Camping Association English Section's first Honorary President, printed in Canadian Camping Vol. 26 No. 1 (Fall 1973), p. 12, gives her service as Executive Secretary of the Jewish Community Camps of Montreal -- Camp B'nai Brith, the Jewish Laurentian Fresh Air Camp and Wooden Acres -- as 1946 to 1949. Her obituary in Canadian Camping Vol. 36 No. 4 (Winter 1985), p. 2, signed by Frances Kelly and Robert Lazanik and clearly reworked from the 1973 text, gives the same service as 1946 to 1969. A single-digit typesetting or OCR slip (4 for 6, or 6 for 4) is the most economical explanation and neither reading is preferred here. Arguments each way: 1946-1969 fits the following sentence, 'During her years in this position, Mrs. Kahn instituted many new projects', and gives a 23-year tenure ending at a plausible retirement; 1946-1949 fits her preceding term as Executive Director of the Young Women's Hebrew Association (1936-1945) and her 1946 arrival in Quebec Camping Association work, and would leave her free for the QCA offices she held from 1958. The point is minor for Kanawana -- Kahn matters to this project as the co-chairman of the Quebec standards committee from 1959-60 -- but it is recorded because the no-silent-overwrite rule applies to small facts as well as large ones.
conflicts.notes: Found by the full word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issue 153. HUMAN DECISION POINT under CLAUDE.md only in the formal sense: two documented sources disagreeing. In practice a scan of the printed 1973 and 1985 pages, or an obituary in the Montreal press for March 1985, would settle it. canadian-camping-movement.md states both readings and points here; neither is used as fact.

conflicts.entity: YMCA Camp Stephens, Lake of the Woods (year camping began) -- and, consequently, Kanawana's rank among Canada's oldest camps
conflicts.description: TWO DOCUMENTED DATES FROM INSIDE THE SAME INSTITUTION, NINETY YEARS APART. (a) 1891: Camp Stephens's own directors -- Grant Platts, Scott McGregor and Juliane Schaible of the Winnipeg YM-YWCA -- wrote in Canadian Camping Magazine Vol. 39 No. 1 (Summer 1987), p. 21: 'Y.M.-Y.W.C.A. Camp Stephens has been providing resident camping experiences for youth since 1891. It is one of the oldest resident camps in North America... Camp Stephens is looking forward to celebrating its 100th anniversary in 1991.' The same issue's 'What's In A Name?' (p. 27) adds: 'Originally known in 1891 as the Lake of the Woods Institute, the Y.M.C.A. Camp Stephens took its present name in 1896.' (b) JULY 1894: T. Duncan Patton -- a founder of Camp Kanawana -- records in his memoir that his first visit to the Lake of the Woods islands was July 1894, 'and from that date on camps were promoted and held annually,' the five islands passing to the Winnipeg YMCA in 1907. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND CAMP STEPHENS: this wiki asserted in three articles that Kanawana (1894) is 'Canada's second-oldest camp, after Big Cove (1889)'. If Camp Stephens has run since 1891, that ordinal is wrong. Taken with Big Cove's own director dating that camp to 1891 (Canadian Camping Magazine Vol. 38 No. 3, Winter 1987, p. 8) against the 1889 and 1890 already recorded in c_-adjacent notes, THREE of the four candidate dates for Canada's oldest camp now fall in 1889-1891, and Kanawana's 1894 follows all of them. A RECONCILIATION SUGGESTS ITSELF and is NOT adopted: the 1891 'Lake of the Woods Institute' may have been a men's conference-encampment rather than a children's resident camp, with youth camping beginning in 1894 as Patton describes. Neither source says so, and adopting it would be inventing the explanation that happens to preserve this project's own camp's ranking. ACTION TAKEN 2026-09-05: the ordinal ranking was WITHDRAWN from canadian-camping-movement.md, quebec-camp-landscape.md and timeline-overview.md, and replaced with 'Quebec's first residential summer camp and among the oldest in Canada', which every source supports. Kanawana's Quebec primacy is not in dispute. NEXT ACTION: ask the YMCA-YWCA of Winnipeg and the Manitoba provincial archives what the Lake of the Woods Institute of 1891 actually was, and whether the 1991 centenary produced a documented history; ask the Camping Association of Nova Scotia and the Halifax YMCA for a primary record of Big Cove's first season.
conflicts.notes: Human decision point under the standing directive: two DOCUMENTED sources disagreeing with each other, not oral history against a document. No resolution is offered. The wiki text has been made safe in the meantime by dropping the claim that depends on the disagreement rather than by choosing a side.

conflicts.description: TWO DOCUMENTED SOURCES, SIX DAYS APART. (a) 4 OCTOBER 1958: wiki/people/hedley-dimock.md states he died 4 October 1958 at Burlingame, San Mateo, California, citing an Oakland Tribune obituary published the following day. (b) 10 OCTOBER 1958: the unsigned Camp Tonakela report in Canadian Camping Vol. 11 No. 4 (June 1959), p. 205, states: "Dr. Hedley S. Dimock passed away at his home in San Francisco, on October 10th, 1958, and a tablet to his memory has been unveiled at the camp." San Francisco against Burlingame is loose usage and not itself a conflict -- Burlingame is a San Francisco suburb. The date is. Source (a) is a contemporary newspaper obituary published the day after the event; source (b) is a memorial notice written eight months later by an organisation Dimock had chaired (he was U.S.A. Chairman of the North American Committee for Camp Tonakela, per Canadian Camping Vol. 12 No. 3, April 1960, p. 136). The next-day obituary is the stronger source and the wiki's date should stand pending resolution, but the discrepancy is recorded rather than silently ignored. Resolving it properly needs a death certificate, a probate record, or a second independent obituary.
conflicts.notes: Human decision point under the standing directive: two documented sources disagreeing with each other, not oral history against a document. No wiki text has been changed; hedley-dimock.md continues to state 4 October 1958 on the strength of the next-day obituary. A minor companion discrepancy in the same source, not separately recorded: Camp Tonakela's own inception is dated 1935 in June 1959, while April 1958 has Taylor Statten opening it in 1938 and its twenty-first birthday falling 21 February 1958 (implying 1937) -- three dates in the same magazine within fifteen months. That one does not bear on Kanawana and is noted here only so a later pass does not re-derive it.

conflicts.entity: The origin point of organized camping in Canada -- four competing printed claims, and Kanawana's place among them
conflicts.description: FOUR DISTINCT CLAIMS PRINTED IN THE SAME MAGAZINE WITHIN FIVE YEARS, NONE RECONCILED BY IT. (a) 1884, OTTAWA: a February 1955 item dates the first Canadian camp to an Ottawa YMCA camp at Golden Lake in 1884. (b) 1893/1908, OTTAWA YWCA: a December 1954 item cites an Ottawa YWCA minute of 1893 and dates Golden Lake camping to 1908 -- contradicting (a) about the same lake and city three months later. (c) 1889, CHANCE HARBOUR: "Ace" Milks, former director of Camp On-Da-Da-Waks at Golden Lake out of the Ottawa YMCA, writing about 1948 and printed February 1959: "The first Canadian Y.M.C.A. boys' camp, so far as we can discover, was organized by the Y.M.C.A. Committee of the Maritime Province and held at Chance Harbour, N.S., in the summer of 1889." Note that this is a hedged claim by a named individual retrieved from an Ontario Camping Association research file -- NOT, as f_2241 previously recorded it, a 1959 position of the Canadian Camping Association. Note also that Chance Harbour is in New Brunswick, not Nova Scotia, and that Big Cove -- the 1889 camp this project already carries with seven facts, and whose own director later dated it to 1891 -- is likewise in New Brunswick. Chance Harbour 1889 and Big Cove 1889 may be one camp under two descriptions or two separate camps; nothing in the record settles it. (d) 1905, NORTHWAY LODGE: Fannie Case's Northway Lodge, April 1955, claimed as "first girls' camp in Canada" -- a narrower claim that may not conflict with the others at all. WHY IT MATTERS: Kanawana's founding, dated July 1894 by T. Duncan Patton, follows (a) and (c) and precedes (d). Any ordinal claim this wiki makes about Kanawana's age depends on which of these is true, and none of them can currently be preferred on the evidence.
conflicts.notes: Human decision point: documented sources disagreeing with each other. Related to c_031 (Camp Stephens 1891 vs 1894), which covers the other half of the same question. The two should probably be resolved together. The wiki has already been made safe by withdrawing the 'Canada's second-oldest camp' ordinal from three articles in favour of 'Quebec's first residential summer camp and among the oldest in Canada'; nothing further should be asserted until the underlying institutional records -- Maritime YMCA committee minutes, Ottawa YMCA and YWCA minute books -- are consulted directly. Corrects the attribution in f_2241, which credited claim (c) to the CCA rather than to Milks.
